title: No-thought
hook: Huineng: no-thought is not blankness but not being stuck to thoughts

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Platform Sutra: a woodcutter from the south who became, as tradition calls him, the sixth patriarch. Your line: the sixth patriarch.

A big station has a departures board. Every few minutes it clicks over: a new train, a new platform, a new city. Nobody standing in the hall gets on every train. Most people glance up, read a line, and keep walking. Some trains they board. Most they let go, and the board doesn't mind either way. Now try that with a mind. Thoughts click over all day: lunch, that email, a worry about Thursday. Huineng had a word for meeting them the way a traveler meets a departures board, and it's probably not what it sounds like.
screen: `A DEPARTURES BOARD.` → `NOBODY BOARDS EVERY TRAIN.` → `THOUGHTS CLICK OVER ALL DAY.`

segments.voice: In the Platform Sutra, Huineng sets out three teachings side by side: no-thought as the doctrine, no-form as the substance, and non-abiding as the root. Today is the first, but they lean on each other. No-thought sounds like an empty head, a mind wiped blank. Huineng says plainly that this is a mistake. Trying to think of nothing at all, cutting off every thought, is in his telling its own kind of trap, a mind tied up by an idea of what meditation should be. So what is it? In paraphrase, he says no-thought means that in the midst of thoughts, you are not carried off by them. Thought follows thought, and none of them is held on to. That's the non-abiding: the mind doesn't move in and live in any one of them. When thoughts don't stick, he says, there is no bondage. So the worry about Thursday can arrive, can even be useful, and then go, the way a train leaves the board. And the senses stay open. Huineng doesn't ask anyone to close their eyes on the world. He describes the senses going out and coming back freely, seeing and hearing everything, while the mind isn't stained by what it meets. No-thought, in his hands, isn't less life. It's full life, with nothing gripping. The same thread the Xinxin Ming was pulling a few days ago, now tied to a teacher's seat: not stuck.
screen: `THREE TEACHINGS, ONE STRAND.` · `NOT A BLANK MIND.` · `THOUGHT AFTER THOUGHT, UNSTUCK.` · `THE SENSES COME AND GO FREELY.` · then, large: `NOT STUCK.`

segments.voice: Don't try to stop thinking; let thoughts come up like lines on a departures board, notice each one, there's a thought, and let it go on without you. If you find you've boarded one and are a few stops down the line in a story, that's fine. Just step off and come back to the breath.
No-thought. Huineng's teaching that the mind can meet every thought without being carried off by any of them. Not blankness. Today's word.
Your line: not stuck. Thoughts can come and go, like trains, without taking you along. Catch you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Zen and Chan teachers often explain Huineng's no-thought in talks on sitting, describing practice as letting thoughts arise and pass without being carried off, rather than forcing the mind blank.
